stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
In trials at forty accounting and software firms, employees moved to a four-day week with no cut in pay. Managers reported that output held steady while sick days and reported burnout fell. Advocates concluded that a shorter week benefits workers and employers alike.

Text 2
The office trials are encouraging, but they may not describe every workplace. When a regional hospital laundry tried the same schedule, its machines still needed staff every day, so the remaining shifts grew longer and output fell by nearly a tenth.
choices: It identifies a workplace where the result reported in Text 1 did not hold.
It offers further evidence that output held steady under a shorter week.
It argues that a four-day week reduces output in nearly every kind of job.
It describes the office trials that the advocates in Text 1 had criticized.
explanation: Text 1 reports a general result: at office firms, output held steady under a four-day week, and advocates say everyone benefits. Text 2 starts by crediting those trials ("encouraging"), then turns to one workplace, a hospital laundry, where output fell. So Text 2 limits the scope of Text 1's claim without rejecting it.

B.why: You picked up the shared topic but missed the turn at "but." At the laundry output fell, so Text 2 does not support the steady-output finding.

C.why: You turned one counterexample into a sweeping rule. Text 2 describes one laundry and calls the office results encouraging, so it never says nearly every job loses output.

D.why: You assigned the wrong role to Text 1. The advocates praised the office trials and did not criticize them. This choice gets Text 2's subject right and Text 1's position wrong.

stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
Between 2015 and 2020, twelve towns installed chilled water fountains in their public parks. Over the same period, surveys showed that children in those towns drank about a third less soda. The researchers therefore concluded that easy access to free water led children to choose it over sugary drinks.

Text 2
No one doubts that soda drinking fell in these towns. Yet most of them also banned soda sales in their schools during those years, and that policy could simply have produced the drop on its own.
choices: It questions whether soda drinking among the children actually declined.
It proposes a different possible cause for the decline described in Text 1.
It presents survey results showing that the fountains raised soda drinking.
It explains the method the researchers in Text 1 used to survey children.
explanation: Text 1 ends with its conclusion ("therefore"): the fountains caused the decline. Text 2 accepts that the decline happened ("No one doubts..."). It then names another explanation, the school soda bans, that "could simply" account for the same result. Text 2 agrees on the observation and offers a different cause.

A.why: You read Text 2 as disagreeing about everything. Its first sentence grants that soda drinking fell. It disputes only the cause.

C.why: You invented a finding that reverses both texts. Neither text reports that soda drinking rose, and Text 2 presents no new survey.

D.why: You fixed on the word "surveys" in Text 1. Text 2 never discusses how the data were gathered. It is about what caused the drop.

stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
Many astronomers think that "hot Jupiters," giant planets that orbit extremely close to their stars, could not have formed there, since too little gas exists so near a star. Instead, these planets are thought to have formed far out and then migrated inward over millions of years.

Text 2
The planet WR-208b offers a telling case. Its orbit is sharply tilted relative to its star's equator, a pattern that a planet forming close in would be unlikely to show but that a long inward journey would readily produce.
choices: It presents a general theory that the planet discussed in Text 1 illustrates.
It describes a planet that appears to have formed close to its own star.
It gives a specific example that is consistent with the view in Text 1.
It explains why astronomers first began searching for giant planets.
explanation: Text 1 states a general view: hot Jupiters formed far out and migrated inward. Text 2 describes one planet, WR-208b ("a telling case"), whose tilted orbit is what a long inward journey would produce. Text 2 is a specific example that supports Text 1's general claim.

A.why: You reversed the roles. Text 1 holds the general theory and Text 2 holds the single planet. Text 1 discusses no specific planet.

B.why: You took the opposite of Text 2's point. Text 2 says a planet forming close in would be unlikely to have this orbit, so WR-208b points toward migration.

D.why: You answered a question neither text raises. The history of planet searches does not appear in Text 2. It is about one planet's orbit.

stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
Seismologists have long cautioned that earthquakes cannot be predicted with any useful precision. Small tremors occur constantly, and only rarely does one turn out to be a foreshock to a major quake, so no one can say in advance when a large rupture will strike.

Text 2
Although the exact timing of large quakes remains beyond reach, warning is still possible. Sensors can detect the fast, weak first waves of a quake that has already begun and send alerts seconds before the slower, damaging waves arrive, time enough to halt trains.
choices: It accepts Text 1's point about prediction but describes another kind of warning.
It claims that new sensors can now predict when large quakes will occur.
It gives an example of a small tremor that turned out to be a foreshock.
It rejects the alert sensors that the seismologists in Text 1 had recommended.
explanation: Text 2 opens with a concession ("Although the exact timing... remains beyond reach"), which agrees with Text 1 that quakes cannot be predicted. It then turns to a different kind of warning: detecting a quake that has already started and alerting people seconds before the damaging waves arrive.

B.why: You missed the concession. Text 2 says timing remains beyond reach. The sensors detect a quake that has already begun and do not predict one.

C.why: You fixed on a detail from Text 1. Foreshocks appear only in Text 1, and Text 2 gives no example of one.

D.why: You attributed something to Text 1 that it does not say. Text 1 never mentions or recommends alert sensors, and Text 2 supports them.

stem: Which choice best describes how Text 2 relates to Text 1?
stimulus:
Text 1
Folklorists studying modern urban legends have argued that such stories spread because they give voice to shared anxieties. Tales of contaminated fast food, for instance, circulated most widely as families began relying on meals prepared by unseen strangers.

Text 2
Nineteenth-century sailors' accounts of sea serpents fit a similar pattern. Reports of the creatures multiplied in decades when shipwrecks were frequent and crossings felt especially perilous, suggesting that the tales expressed fears crews could not otherwise name.
choices: It disputes Text 1's claim that legends express widely shared anxieties.
It extends the explanation in Text 1 to stories from an earlier period.
It offers the general theory that the examples in Text 1 then illustrate.
It argues that sailors' reports of sea serpents were largely accurate.
explanation: Text 1 explains that legends spread because they express shared anxieties, and it gives a modern example. Text 2 says sailors' tales "fit a similar pattern" and applies the same explanation to stories from the 1800s. Text 2 extends Text 1's idea to an earlier era.

A.why: You missed the agreement signal. "Fit a similar pattern" tells you Text 2 accepts Text 1's explanation and uses it.

C.why: You reversed which text does what. Text 1 states the general theory, and Text 2 supplies another case of it.

D.why: You read in a claim Text 2 never makes. It treats the sightings as expressions of fear and never says the serpents were real.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
In the early 1800s, English handloom weavers saw their earnings collapse. Many historians have traced this hardship to the power loom, which could produce several times as much cloth per worker as a handloom. Thus, they argue, the machine itself drove the weavers into poverty.

Text 2
There is no question that power looms outpaced handlooms. But weavers' wages were already falling in the 1810s, when few power looms were running. A more likely cause is that thousands of new workers, drawn by earlier high pay, had crowded into the trade.
choices: The power loom was the main cause of handloom weavers' poverty.
Weavers' wages fell because too many workers entered the trade.
Power looms could produce cloth faster than handlooms could.
Few power looms were operating in England before the 1830s.
explanation: Text 1 says the power loom produced several times as much cloth per worker. Text 2 opens by granting that point: "There is no question that power looms outpaced handlooms." The authors disagree about why wages fell, but both accept that power looms were faster. That shared ground is choice C.

A.why: You took Text 1's conclusion and assumed both authors hold it. Text 2 argues against it and blames an oversupply of workers instead. You got one text's role right and the other's wrong.

B.why: You took Text 2's explanation and gave it to both authors. Text 1 blames the machine, not the number of workers, so its author would not agree.

D.why: Text 2 only says few power looms were running in the 1810s. Neither text says anything about the 1830s, so you stretched a claim about one decade to cover a later one.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Over the past four decades, weather forecasts have grown steadily more accurate. Satellites now track moisture and wind over oceans that once went unobserved, feeding richer data into forecasting models. A forecaster can therefore now plan a full week ahead with confidence.

Text 2
Gains in forecasting are real, but they are uneven. Individual thunderstorms form within hours from small pockets of rising air, too small for most models to capture. For a town wondering whether a storm will strike tomorrow afternoon, a forecast is still little more than an estimate of the odds.
choices: Weather forecasts have become more accurate in recent decades.
Forecasts are now dependable a week ahead for any kind of weather.
Satellite data has done little to improve forecasting models.
Thunderstorms have become harder to predict than they once were.
explanation: Text 1 describes forecasts growing steadily more accurate. Text 2 begins "Gains in forecasting are real" before limiting the claim to exclude thunderstorms. Text 2 narrows Text 1 without rejecting it, so both authors accept that forecasting has improved.

B.why: This is a stronger form of Text 1's final sentence, and it is exactly the claim Text 2 limits. Text 2 shows that storms still can't be predicted with confidence even a day ahead, so its author would reject "any kind of weather."

C.why: Text 1 credits satellite data with the improvement, and Text 2 does not dispute it. This choice reverses what Text 1 says.

D.why: Text 2 says thunderstorms are still hard to predict, not that they have become harder. Neither text compares storm forecasts now with those of the past.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
In a survey of 3,000 adults, researchers found that people who ate breakfast every day weighed less, on average, than people who regularly skipped it. The team concluded that a morning meal helps regulate appetite, keeping people from overeating later in the day.

Text 2
The link between breakfast and lower body weight in such surveys is consistent, but it may say nothing about breakfast itself. People who eat breakfast daily also tend to keep regular sleep schedules and exercise more often. Those habits could simply account for the difference.
choices: A morning meal keeps people from overeating later in the day.
Breakfast eaters weigh less mainly because they exercise more.
Body weight in the survey was unrelated to breakfast habits.
People who ate breakfast daily tended to weigh less on average.
explanation: Text 2 does not dispute what the survey found. It calls the link "consistent" and offers a different explanation for it. Both authors accept the finding that daily breakfast eaters weighed less on average. They disagree only about why.

A.why: This is Text 1's explanation, the claim Text 2 was written to question. You assumed Text 2 responds by agreeing when it actually offers another cause.

B.why: Text 2 only says these habits "could" explain the difference. You turned a possibility into a firm conclusion, and Text 1's author would not accept it either way.

C.why: Both texts say breakfast eaters weighed less on average. Calling weight "unrelated" contradicts the finding that both authors accept.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
Many coaches have athletes hold long, still stretches before training. Yet studies find that holding a stretch for a minute or more briefly reduces the force a muscle can produce. Sports scientists therefore conclude that athletes should drop these static stretches from their warm-ups.

Text 2
For sprinters and jumpers, who rely on explosive force, the case against static stretching before competition is convincing. Gymnasts and dancers are another matter. Their events demand extreme flexibility, and for them a slight loss of power is a fair price for the range of motion stretching provides.
choices: Every athlete should remove static stretches from warm-ups.
Long static stretches can briefly reduce a muscle's force.
Flexibility matters more than power in most sports.
Static stretching before competition helps sprinters perform.
explanation: Text 1 reports that long stretches briefly reduce muscle force. Text 2 accepts this. It calls the case "convincing" for sprinters and refers to "a slight loss of power" for gymnasts. It disagrees only about whether every athlete should drop stretching, so the reduced force is what both authors share.

A.why: This is Text 1's broad conclusion, which Text 2 narrows by pointing to gymnasts and dancers. You treated a claim that Text 2 limits as one it accepts.

C.why: Text 2 says flexibility outweighs power only for gymnasts and dancers. Neither author makes a claim about "most sports."

D.why: Both texts say static stretching hurts sprinters' explosive force. This choice says the opposite.

stem: Based on the texts, both authors would most likely agree with which statement?
stimulus:
Text 1
In early 2020, the red star Betelgeuse faded to less than half its usual brightness, a larger drop than any recorded in a century of observation. Because massive stars become unstable near the end of their lives, some observers suggested that the fading signaled Betelgeuse was about to explode as a supernova.

Text 2
Betelgeuse's dimming was real and remarkable, but it need not point to an approaching explosion. The star regularly sheds gas into space, and that gas can cool into dust. A cloud of dust drifting between the star and Earth could simply have blocked part of its light.
choices: Betelgeuse's fading showed that it was about to become a supernova.
Dust shed by Betelgeuse has blocked its light many times before.
Betelgeuse grew noticeably fainter than usual in early 2020.
Betelgeuse's brightness in 2020 stayed within its usual range.
explanation: Text 2 begins by granting Text 1's observation: the dimming "was real and remarkable." It then offers dust as another explanation. The texts disagree about the cause, but both accept that Betelgeuse faded noticeably in early 2020.

A.why: This is the supernova idea from the end of Text 1, and Text 2 was written to question it. You read the concession as agreement and missed the turn at "but."

B.why: Text 2 says only that dust could have dimmed the star this time. Nothing in either text says this has happened "many times before."

D.why: Text 1 calls the drop the largest in a century, and Text 2 calls it remarkable. Both describe a change far outside the star's usual range.
